How can there be any stability? Would you rather not even look at me? <gloss>Narrative mode</gloss>


The character <term>mao</term> <gloss>to cover/overshadow</gloss> is derived from the radical for "eye."
The pronunciation follows the sounds <term>hu</term> and <term>dao</term> <note>phonetic gloss</note>.
The pronunciation follows the sound <term>bao</term> <note>phonetic gloss</note>.


Oh, Sun! Oh, Moon! You overshadow the world below. But as for that man, he has gone away and no longer loves me. How can there be any stability? Would you rather not even requite me? <gloss>Narrative mode</gloss>

Oh, Sun! Oh, Moon! You emerge from the East. But as for that man, his reputation and words are not good. How can there be any stability? He has caused me to be forgotten. <gloss>Narrative mode</gloss>

Oh, Sun! Oh, Moon! From the East you emerge. Oh, Father! Oh, Mother! You did not nurture me to the end. How can there be any stability? His response to me does not follow the proper path. <gloss>Narrative mode. Lady Zhuang Jiang was not answered with affection by Duke Zhuang. Therefore, she cried out to the sun and moon to voice her grievance, and composed this poem.</gloss>

<gloss>This poem</gloss>
"Sun and Moon" consists of four stanzas. Each stanza has six lines.

<summary>This page contains the final three stanzas of the poem Sun and Moon from the Odes of Bei. The text expresses the grief of a neglected wife, identified by tradition as Lady Zhuang Jiang, who appeals to the celestial bodies regarding her husband's inconstancy.</summary>
